title: Sending data and saying what kind it is

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. run.js starts the cupboard server, runs your functions against it and prints every request and answer.

tasks.title: Add a song request
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/send.js`, make `addRequest(base, song, from)` ask the server at `base` to add a song request:

- a `POST` to the path `/api/requests`
- whose body is JSON: an object with `song` and `from`, and nothing else
- whose `content-type` says the body is JSON

The server answers with JSON about the new request. `addRequest` gives back the `id` in that answer.

Check starts a server of its own, sends songs with quotes and other characters in them, and looks at the method, the `content-type` and the body its server received, and at the id `addRequest` gave back.
nextSteps: Hand `fetch` the method, the headers and the body in its options.
Write the body with the method that turns a value into JSON text.
Read the answer as JSON and take the id from it.
Run `node run.js` and read the request it prints: the body is under the headers.
hints: Three things in the options: the method that adds, a `content-type` header, and the body as JSON text. Without the header, `fetch` labels a text body as plain text, and the server answers 415.
`JSON.stringify({ song, from })` writes the object as JSON, quotes and all. The JSON type is `application/json`.
`fetch(new URL('/api/requests', base), { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ song, from }) })`, then `return (await response.json()).id`.

tasks.title: Read where the new request lives
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `requestAddress(base, song, from)` send the same request as `addRequest`, and give back the whole address of the new song request as text, built from the `location` header of the answer. The `location` may be a whole address or only a path on the server that answered.

Check starts a server of its own that answers with a path in `location` once and with whole addresses twice, and compares the address `requestAddress` gave back with where its server said the request lives.
nextSteps: Send the same request as in Task 1.
Read the `location` header of the answer, and print it.
Turn it into a whole address, whether it is a path or already whole.
Run `node run.js`: the cupboard server answers with a path.
hints: The server decides where a new thing lives, and says so in `location`. Do not build the address from the id yourself.
A location that is only a path means the same server. `new URL` with a second value joins a path to it, and leaves a whole address as it is.
`return new URL(response.headers.get('location'), base).href`, after the same `fetch` as Task 1.

tasks.title: Say whether it was added, and why not
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `tryRequest(base, song, from)` send the same request as `addRequest`, and give back:

- `{ added: true, id }` when the answer is `201`, with the id from the answer
- `{ added: false, reason }` when the answer is a client error, where `reason` is the `error` the server wrote in its JSON

Check starts a server of its own that answers `201` once and refuses with client errors of its own, each with its own reason.
nextSteps: Send the same request as in Task 1.
Read the body as JSON once, whatever the status.
Decide by the status which of the two objects to give back.
Run `node run.js`: Bram's request is already on the list, and one request has no name.
hints: A refusal is still an answer with a JSON body. The reason is in that body, not in the status line.
Read the JSON before you decide, then give back `added` with either the `id` or the `error` from it.
`const answer = await response.json()`, then `if (response.status === 201) return { added: true, id: answer.id }` and otherwise `return { added: false, reason: answer.error }`.
